head:
Profiles · Midlife

Getting back to sport between 45 and 64: a plan, what changes at this age, and above all how to stick with it

A blood pressure reading to keep an eye on, a belt that feels tight, knees that ache: in general we know what we should be doing. The underlying plan looks like everyone else's. What changes at this age is the starting point, the dose, what you avoid, the obstacles and the moment to ask for medical advice. This article follows a typical person through to a 12-week plan, distinguishing what is demonstrated from what is a proposal.

The question

Illustrative profile, not a real case

A 52-year-old. She played sport when she was younger, then work, children or ageing parents took over, and it has been years since she trained regularly. She gets more out of breath on the stairs than she used to. At the last check-up, her blood pressure was “to be monitored”. Her belt feels tight although the scales have barely moved. A knee or a shoulder aches in the morning. Her sleep is worse. If she is a woman, it may be perimenopause; if he is a man, he wonders whether it is “age” or “testosterone”.

She is afraid of getting injured or feeling faint, and she has already restarted several times without sticking to it. She is not looking for a tailor-made programme, which would need someone in front of her, but for the order of things, the doses, what to avoid and a way to keep going.

The question

When you resume activity between 45 and 64 after years of stopping, what really changes at this age, what should you do concretely week after week, and how do you make it last?

What is at stake

First the trajectory: strength, power, endurance and bone decline at different speeds, and what you do between 40 and 60 affects what you will be able to do at 70 (article “How the body ages”); women also go through a hormonal window (article “Menopause and declining testosterone: what training makes up for, and what it does not”). Then cardiovascular health: blood pressure and waist circumference are the first signals, and acting costs least at that point (a line of reasoning, not a study result).

There are two ways to go wrong: starting too abruptly after a long break, or waiting until you are ready and never starting. And there is the real bottleneck: sticking with it. The plan fits on one page and the knowledge is accessible; what makes the difference is repetition, with patience. We proceed in four steps, from the general to the specific, then the obstacles, the plan and the answer.

Step 1 of 4 · The underlying plan

The underlying plan is the same for everyone, and what this age changes lies elsewhere

For adults aged 18 to 64, the World Health Organization (2020) recommends 150 to 300 minutes per week of moderate endurance, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous intensity, and strengthening of the major muscle groups on at least two days per week. It adds that doing a little is better than nothing and that you should build up gradually.15,16 European cardiologists (ESC, 2020) say the same thing: at least 150 minutes moderate or 75 vigorous, working up towards 300 minutes (class I, level A), over 4 to 5 days, and 2 to 3 strength sessions.2

What this means

The target does not change with age in this range. What changes is the route to reach it.

DimensionWhat changes at 45-64
Starting pointYears of stopping: the build-up towards the target takes more weeks (a ramp-up stage to plan for).
RisksMedical advice according to specific criteria, including age (HAS: 45 and over and a plan for near-maximal intensity). Risk of sudden intense effort in sedentary people (step 2).1,6
What to avoidHigh intensity without a habit, maximal loads straight away, jumps without preparation (THW proposal).
Obstacles, hormonesTime, fatigue, pain at the start, past failures (part 3); women: priority to loading; men: no hormonal shortcut (“Menopause and declining testosterone: what training makes up for, and what it does not”).

The demonstrations are in “How the body ages” (what declines), “Menopause and declining testosterone: what training makes up for, and what it does not” (hormones), “Muscular strength, the forgotten health insurance” (strength) and “Cardio and lifespan: what the data show, and what they do not show” (endurance): only the practical conclusions are kept. That leaves the most sensitive point: starting without putting yourself at risk.

Step 2 of 4 · Getting back after years of stopping

The risk lies in the abrupt start, not in the activity itself

Mittleman and colleagues asked 1,228 patients who had had a heart attack what they had been doing in the preceding hour, and compared it with their usual frequency of intense exertion. On average, intense exertion goes with a heart attack risk 5.9 times higher in the following hour. This average hides the essential point.6

The more accustomed you are to exertion, the less an intense effort triggers a heart attack

Relative risk of heart attack in the hour following intense exertion, according to usual frequency of intense exertion. Source: Mittleman et al., NEJM, 1993 (abstract).6

What this means

Among those who exert themselves intensely less than once a week, the risk in the following hour is multiplied by 107; among those who do so five times or more, by 2.4. This is the profile of someone resuming after a long break: the danger lies in the first violent effort, not in brisk walking. A meta-analysis of 12 studies of the same type (19,891 patients) points the same way: risk multiplied by 3.46 with episodic exertion, and about 43% lower relative risk for each additional weekly occasion of activity.7 A relative risk is not an absolute risk: an information page cites one sudden death per 1.51 million episodes of exertion in men (second-hand figure).8

What the HAS and the ESC say about resuming

The Haute Autorité de santé starts from a 7-question questionnaire (Q-AAP+, the French version of the PAR-Q+). Seven “no” answers: you can start being more active. One “yes”: medical advice is recommended beforehand. The case that concerns your age: at 45 and over, without regular intense activity, with a plan for intensity close to maximal, advice is recommended.1,4,5 For the rest, inactive people start at low or moderate intensity and increase gradually, walking can be started without consulting if there are no symptoms, and the majority of patients do not need a consultation. The HAS considers the exercise test to be poorly predictive in the absence of symptoms. It lists among high risks known cardiovascular disease, diabetes (with exceptions), moderate to severe kidney failure, total cholesterol above 3.1 g/L, blood pressure of 180/110 mmHg or more.1

The ESC goes the same way: for low or moderate risk, leisure-time activity can be considered without further evaluation, and sedentary people can do low-intensity exercise without evaluation (class IIa, level C). For a sedentary person planning intensive exercise or competition, an evaluation with a maximal exercise test should be considered (class IIa, level C). In athletes over 35, the majority of sudden deaths are attributed to coronary artery disease.2,3

The two sources converge: the sensitive point is high intensity, not resuming. A gentle start, without symptoms and with seven “no” answers, does not call for a systematic check-up; a “yes”, a symptom or a high risk calls for advice beforehand. Hence a gradual build-up, with high intensity kept for the end. The remaining question is whether the heart responds to this work at this age.

Step 3 of 4 · The heart, the arteries and weight

At this age, the heart and arteries still respond to regular training

Howden and colleagues (Levine's team, Circulation, 2018) followed 61 sedentary adults with an average age of 53 (48% men), of whom 53 completed the study. For two years, one group did supervised training of at least 30 minutes, 4 to 5 days per week, including at least one session of intense intervals; the other did a light 3-day programme (yoga, balance, strength).9,10

Two years of regular training increase the endurance of sedentary 53-year-olds

Mean VO2max before and after two years. The increase of about 18% is the one published; the unit is not specified in the abstracts read. Source: Howden et al., Circulation, 2018 (abstracts).9,10

What this means

The trained group gained about 18% in VO2max, the other stayed stable, and left ventricular stiffness fell in the trained group only (0.072 to 0.051, against 0.0635 to 0.062). Limits: small trial, two supervised years (88% adherence), comparison with a light programme and not with nothing. At 53, after a sedentary life, the heart therefore still changes with regular practice; protection against heart failure is only a hypothesis of the authors.

Blood pressure is the signal many people receive at this age. A meta-analysis of 93 randomised trials (5,223 adults) measured the effect of training according to the starting level.11

Training lowers blood pressure mostly when it is already high

Net change in systolic blood pressure (mmHg), with 95% confidence interval. “Slightly high blood pressure” corresponds to the “prehypertensive” category of the study. Values from the article's table (the abstract gives −4.0 for resistance training with slightly high blood pressure). Source: Cornelissen and Smart, J Am Heart Assoc, 2013.11

What this means

When blood pressure is high, endurance lowers systolic pressure by about 8 mmHg (and diastolic by about 5). When it is slightly high, the drop is 2 with endurance and 4 with resistance training. When it is normal, nothing clear. These are group averages, and a person on treatment does not change their treatment alone. The clearest effect comes from moderate intensity. Men had a larger drop than women with endurance: one subgroup among many, to be read as a lead.

For weight, a Cochrane review of 43 trials (3,476 adults) concludes that exercise alone leads to little weight loss; added to a diet, it leads to about 1.0 kg more (from 0.7 to 1.3).12 Exercise is a poor tool for losing weight on its own, and a good tool for what the scales do not see (“Menopause and declining testosterone: what training makes up for, and what it does not”).

Step 4 of 4 · Muscles, bones and joints

What is specific to this age: progressive loading, and pain as information

For muscle, the article “Muscular strength, the forgotten health insurance” made the demonstration: about 30 to 60 minutes of strength training per week, bodyweight included, in addition to endurance. The article “How the body ages” shows that strength goes faster than mass, so it has to be measured, and the article “Menopause and declining testosterone: what training makes up for, and what it does not” that in postmenopausal women heavy, supervised loading produced gains in strength and density at some sites. These conclusions underpin the strength part of the plan. The question specific to this age lies elsewhere: pain. A Cochrane review of 54 trials on knee osteoarthritis, summarised by McMaster Optimal Aging, measured the effect of an exercise programme (leg strengthening, aerobic exercise, walking).13

In knee osteoarthritis, exercise reduces pain and improves function, with an effect that fades

Mean improvement on a 100-point scale, with 95% confidence interval. The grey points beyond 6 months are fragile: the effect on pain disappears when two trials with very different results are removed. Source: Fransen et al., Cochrane, 2015 (summarised by McMaster Optimal Aging).13

What this means

Just after a programme, pain is improved by about 12 points out of 100 and function by about 10; two to six months later, by about 6 and 3. Knee pain is therefore not a reason to stop all exercise: exercise here is a modest treatment, which requires you to keep going. This applies to diagnosed knee osteoarthritis, not to all pain.

How do you dose when it hurts? Silbernagel and colleagues tested a “pain-monitoring model” on 38 patients with Achilles tendinopathy: no more than 5 out of 10 during exertion, pain after exertion back down by the next morning, and neither pain nor stiffness rising from one week to the next. Those who continued under this rule improved as much as those who rested for six weeks. The trial is small, read via a clinic summary, and concerns one tendon: carrying the rule over to all joints is a proposal, which the plan adopts with a margin.14

What changes depending on whether you are a woman or a man

  • Women, perimenopause and menopause. Priority to progressive strength and, when tolerated and cleared, to impact loading, because this is what the trials test for bone (“Menopause and declining testosterone: what training makes up for, and what it does not”). Follow-up by tests rather than by the scales. Hormone therapy is a medical decision, which is not in opposition to training. These trials involve postmenopausal women (65 years on average in the most telling one): transposition to age 50 has not been directly tested.
  • Men. The decline in testosterone is slow and variable, and training is not judged by its ability to raise it (“Menopause and declining testosterone: what training makes up for, and what it does not”). Blood pressure and waist circumference to monitor; VO2max falls faster in men from their forties in the follow-up of the article “How the body ages”, hence the importance of maintaining endurance.
  • In both cases, a troublesome symptom (intense hot flushes, unusually low desire, persistent fatigue) is a matter for a consultation, not for a programme. Doses, phases and tests remain the same.

The real obstacles, and how to remove them

A sound plan that is not applied is worth nothing. The typical obstacles at this age: time (work, family, relatives to help), fatigue, the discomfort of the first sessions, “too late”, aborted restarts, comparison with yourself at 25. Research focuses mostly on the levers.

The time it takes to build a habit. Lally and colleagues asked 96 volunteers to repeat one action every day (eating, drinking or exercising) in the same context for 84 days. Of the 39 curves that could be modelled, the automaticity plateau was reached in a median of 66 days (from 18 to 254); for exercise, 91 days (central 50% from 44 to 118), with no significant difference from the other actions. A single missed occasion had little effect.17,18

It takes weeks, sometimes months, for an action to become automatic, with wide variation

Estimated time to reach 95% of the automaticity plateau (modelling). Bars: central 50%; dot: median. Beyond 84 days, these are extrapolations. Source: Lally et al., Eur J Soc Psychol, 2010, read via a summary page.17

What this means

Twelve weeks is the order of magnitude for installing an action, not a guarantee: some people get there in 3 weeks, others in 8 months. Gardner and colleagues advise about 10 weeks of repetition in a stable context (same time, same place), starting small and adding an action rather than forbidding yourself one.18 Limit: participants mostly students, 27 years old on average.

Deciding in advance when and where. A meta-analysis of 94 tests (Gollwitzer and Sheeran) finds that an intention of the type “if this situation, then this action” improves goal attainment (d = 0.65, all goals combined).19 For physical activity, a meta-analysis of randomised trials finds a more modest effect, of 0.25 (0.05 to 0.45).20 For example: “If it is Tuesday, Thursday or Saturday at 7 a.m., then I walk for 25 minutes”.

Measuring. Michie and colleagues (122 evaluations, 44,747 participants) find an average effect of 0.31 for interventions on activity and diet, and of 0.42 (against 0.26) when self-monitoring is combined with another technique, such as a goal.21 With a pedometer (26 studies, adults aged 49 on average), activity increases by about 27%; a step goal predicted the increase.22,23 Among 50-64-year-olds, a review of 55 articles cites among the drivers goals, the belief that activity does you good and social influences.24

What this means

Each lever has an average effect, neither zero nor magical, and they add up. The plan retains four: a slot set in advance, a tiny version for difficult days, a regular measurement, someone to talk to about it. It is not a matter of motivation: it is a system that works on the days when you do not feel like it, and repetition does the rest.

The 12-week action plan

Status. Generic proposal, built from the benchmarks read (WHO, ESC, HAS, articles “Cardio and lifespan: what the data show, and what they do not show”, “Muscular strength, the forgotten health insurance”, “How the body ages”, “Menopause and declining testosterone: what training makes up for, and what it does not”) and not tested as such. The gains cited above come from trials, not from this programme. It replaces neither medical advice nor a coach who sees you move. Minutes, sets and thresholds are drafting choices.

Week 0: before starting

  1. Complete the questionnaire (Q-AAP+ or PAR-Q+).Seven “no” answers: you can start slowly. A “yes”, a symptom or a high risk: medical advice first (step 2).
  2. Do the three tests on the page, under the same conditions.Endurance, strength, balance or mobility; same time of day, same warm-up. This is a starting point, not a verdict. Also note your blood pressure and waist circumference if you know them.
  3. Set your slots and your plan B.Three endurance slots and two strength slots, written as “if... then...”. Plan B for difficult days: 10 minutes of brisk walking or light strength work. A plan B done is better than a full session cancelled.

The load rises in steps, with a lighter week at the end of each phase

THW proposal of weekly minutes over 12 weeks, not tested as such. Moderate aerobic at the bottom of each bar, strength training above (warm-up included, within the 30 to 60 minute range read in the article “Muscular strength, the forgotten health insurance”). The 150-minute benchmark is that of the WHO and the ESC. The totals are additions.

Phase 1 · Establish (weeks 1 to 4)

Goal: regularity, not performance.

  • Endurance: 3 sessions of 20 to 25 minutes at moderate intensity (brisk walking, easy cycling), i.e. 60 to 90 minutes per week. Practical benchmark: you speak in full sentences, you do not sing (common, not sourced here). The HAS places moderate between 3 and less than 6 METs.1
  • Strength: 2 sessions of 20 to 25 minutes, 6 to 7 movements (getting up from a chair, pushing, pulling, hip hinge, plank, calves), 2 sets of 8 to 12 repetitions with 2 to 3 repetitions in reserve. No maximal load.
  • Mobility: 5 minutes on strength days. Week 4: lighter week.
  • To move on to phase 2: 80% of planned sessions over 3 weeks, pain of 3 out of 10 at most and gone by the next day, stable sleep and energy.

Phase 2 · Build up (weeks 5 to 8)

Goal: reach 150 minutes of endurance and load the strength work.

  • Endurance: 110 to 150 minutes in 4 sessions, including a longer one (30 to 45 minutes). The build-up towards 150 is gradual, as the WHO and the ESC recommend.2,15
  • Strength: 2 sessions of 30 minutes, 3 sets; you increase the load when you finish all the sets with 2 repetitions in reserve. Women: heavier loads earlier (5 to 8 repetitions on squat, deadlift, press), clean technique, in line with the trials on bone (“Menopause and declining testosterone: what training makes up for, and what it does not”). Men: same progression.
  • Light impact (especially perimenopause and menopause): uphill walking, stairs. Jumps with a controlled landing wait until phase 3, if knees and back are pain-free (caution proposed).
  • Week 8: lighter week. To move on to phase 3: same criteria, and about 150 minutes sustained without pain that worsens.

Phase 3 · Consolidate (weeks 9 to 12)

Goal: 150 to 180 minutes of endurance, one more sustained session, retests.

  • Endurance: 150 to 180 minutes. One session can become more sustained (for example 4 times 2 to 3 minutes fairly hard, you can only say a few words, with 2 easy minutes in between). The Howden trial included one interval session per week (protocol not detailed in the abstracts read): an inspiration. It assumes seven “no” answers on the questionnaire, and advice if you are 45 or over and aim for an intensity close to maximal.1,9
  • Strength: 2 sessions of 30 minutes, 3 to 4 sets on the major movements, 6 to 10 repetitions. Jumps with a controlled landing possible (women) if cleared and pain-free.
  • Week 12: lighter week, then retests.

After week 12: maintain

  • At least 150 minutes of endurance and 2 strength sessions, with variety.
  • After more than 2 weeks off, resume one phase lower (proposal). The article “How the body ages” quantifies what stopping costs endurance and how quickly it comes back.

Retests, and decisions

WhenWhat, and how to read it
Before week 1The three tests. One measurement locates you, two measurements show a trajectory.
Week 6 (optional)A single test, to adjust: the difference may remain within measurement noise.
Week 12The three tests, same conditions. A difference below the usual variation of the test proves nothing: the article “Cardio and lifespan: what the data show, and what they do not show” cites about 52 metres on the Cooper test, in runners.
AfterwardsEvery 3 to 6 months (proposed rhythm; “Cardio and lifespan: what the data show, and what they do not show” mentions 8 to 12 weeks, “How the body ages” one to two years for the slope).
DecisionProposed criterion
Move forward80% of sessions over 3 weeks, pain of 3 out of 10 at most and gone by the next day, stable sleep and energy.
Stay one more weekA single criterion missed.
Step back one phasePain above 5 out of 10 during exertion, or still there the next day, or rising from one week to the next (Silbernagel principle, transposed), unusual fatigue, or two weeks missed.14
Stop and consultA warning sign (next section).

Sticking with it: the rules of the system

  1. Never two sessions missed in a row.A single missed occasion had little weight in the Lally study; two is the start of a stop. This is what plan B is for.17
  2. A 2-minute log:date, duration, effort from 1 to 10, pain from 0 to 10. Self-monitoring combined with a goal does best in the Michie meta-analysis.21
  3. A concrete goal and someone to talk to about it.Climbing two flights of stairs without stopping, with a partner or a group, and taking stock at 4, 8 and 12 weeks.24

Common mistakes, warning signs, when to consult

  • Starting again as at 25. This is the scenario where the relative risk of step 2 is highest.
  • Betting everything on cardio: strength training has effects that endurance does not replace (“Muscular strength, the forgotten health insurance”, “Menopause and declining testosterone: what training makes up for, and what it does not”).
  • Judging by the scales: exercise alone leads to little weight loss (Cochrane), and body composition changes without the weight moving (“Menopause and declining testosterone: what training makes up for, and what it does not”).
  • Ignoring pain that is rising, or stopping at the first discomfort: exercise reduces osteoarthritic knee pain, and pain that worsens is a signal.
  • Waiting for motivation, or making up all at once the volume missed after a break.

Warning signs. Chest pain, unexplained breathlessness, palpitations, calf pain when walking: the HAS asks that you do not start or continue before seeing a doctor, and the ESC a reassessment in case of symptoms on exertion.1,2 Any new symptom falls into this category, as does swelling, locking or night-time pain in a joint (drafting caution, not a citation).

Medical advice before starting (texts read): a “yes” on the questionnaire; a symptom; known cardiovascular disease, diabetes, moderate to severe kidney failure, total cholesterol above 3.1 g/L or blood pressure of 180/110 mmHg or more; a plan for high intensity at 45 and over without regular intense practice.1,2 Menopause symptoms, unusually low desire, persistent fatigue: consultation too.

The answer to the question

What is solid. The targets are those of all adults: 150 to 300 minutes of moderate endurance and strength training twice a week, building up gradually (WHO, ESC). The risk of sudden intense effort is concentrated in those who almost never do any and decreases with habit (association). HAS and ESC converge: gentle resumption without a heavy work-up when the questionnaire is clear, advice according to specific criteria, caution about high intensity. At 53, two years of training raised endurance in a small randomised trial; endurance lowers blood pressure mostly when it is high; exercise modestly reduces osteoarthritic knee pain.

What is a proposal. The 12-week trajectory and its minutes, the pain thresholds, the sustained session of phase 3, the retests, the woman-man adjustments, plan B, the “never two sessions missed” rule: consistent with the sources, never tested as a programme.

What is not demonstrated. That this plan reduces heart attacks, fractures or mortality (the data on deaths come from observational studies, “Cardio and lifespan: what the data show, and what they do not show” and “Muscular strength, the forgotten health insurance”); that a habit sets in within 12 weeks for everyone; that the trials on bone in postmenopausal women apply to perimenopause; that the pain rule for the Achilles tendon holds for all joints; that it improves sleep or hot flushes (“Menopause and declining testosterone: what training makes up for, and what it does not”). No trial read tests this precise programme.

The plan fits in a few lines: a little regular volume, strength, cautious progression, measurements, recovery. At this age, it asks above all for patience and a start without brutality. The hardest part is not knowing it, it is starting again the following week, then the one after.

What these figures do not say
  • Several sources are abstracts, summary pages or specialist press, and the studies on habit rarely concern 45-64-year-olds alone.17,20
  • Averages describe groups: a one-hour relative risk is not your absolute risk, and a two-year trial is not a twelve-week programme.6,9 This text does not replace medical advice.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need an exercise test before resuming?

Not systematically. The HAS considers it poorly predictive in the absence of symptoms; the ESC suggests considering an evaluation with an exercise test mainly for an intensive plan. A “yes” on the questionnaire or a symptom: talk to a doctor.1,2

I have done nothing for ten years: is it too late?

Nothing that was read suggests so: in the Howden trial, sedentary 53-year-olds gained endurance in two years. Your starting point will be lower than your memories, and the plan takes this into account.9

I miss a week: do I have to start all over?

No: a single missed occasion had little weight in the Lally study. After more than two weeks off, the plan proposes resuming one phase lower, which is a proposal and not a result.17,18

The figures that come from them are not repeated here, except with an explicit reference.
